title: Forward-KL Convergence of Time-Inhomogeneous Langevin Diffusions
claim: Across path speeds, annealing schemes with richer paths reach lower stationary error than plain Langevin, though none match direct sampling.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared y-axis, one legend on top
description: A single row of four line plots, one for each traversal speed T = 0.1, 1, 2 and 10. A shared legend across the top names six methods by color: Direct sample (red), ULA (blue), Dilation (green), Tempering (orange), Convolution (purple) and DAZ (brown). Every panel plots forward KL on a log y-axis, from about 10^-2 to 10^1, against iteration k up to 1e5. All curves drop sharply early and then flatten. Red direct-sample noise sits lowest at about 4e-3. Purple and brown curves plateau near 2e-2. Orange sits higher, green higher still, and blue ULA is highest and flat. At T = 10 the green curve decays slowly after a bump. The eye goes first to the legend, then to the separation between the plateau levels.
caption: Forward-Kullback--Leiber divergence between the sample distribution and the one-dimensional Gaussian-mixture target in terms of the iteration for different paths and traversal speeds controlled by the parameter $T$. Direct sample: A sample of the same size as used in the other schemes, directly drawn from the Gaussian mixture.
abstract: Many practical samplers rely on time-dependent drifts -- often induced by annealing or tempering schedules -- to improve exploration and stability. This motivates a unified non-asymptotic analysis of the corresponding Langevin diffusions and their discretizations. We provide a convergence analysis that includes non-asymptotic bounds for the continuous-time diffusion and its Euler--Maruyama discretization in the forward-Kullback--Leibler divergence under a single set of abstract conditions on the time-dependent drift. The results apply to many practically-relevant annealing schemes, including geometric tempering and annealed Langevin sampling. In addition, we provide numerical experiments comparing the annealing schemes covered by our theory in low- and high-dimensional settings.
